newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean economy heads for rockier end to 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean economy heads for rockier end to 1996.

text.p: The South Korean economy, once a darling of Asia, appears headed for an even rockier end than expected to 1996 as labour strife and other woes loom.
Even South Korean leader Kim Young-sam was realistic enough this weekend not to predict an upswing before the end of next year.
"The economy has its own ups and downs," Kim said in a Saturday interview with the Christian Broadcasting System.

The president cited "high wages and expenses" as the major reason behind the current economic slowdown, which has seen the stock market slump to a 38-month low and dragged down gross domestic product growth.

In a bid to get some momentum going, the government last Tuesday proposed new labour laws to remove authoritarian control and help firms improve competitiveness by giving them more flexibility on staffing.
But the announcement, the first reforms in 43 years, did not go down well with unions and the stock market reacted to the threat of strikes by keeping its downward path.
The country's two major union groups denounced the reforms as aimed at helping business, not protecting workers rights.
They announced strikes unless the government backed down from the plans, an unlikely prospect.

The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions plans a partial strike on December 13 and a full strike three days later, while the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the nation's largest union organisation, plans a one-hour strike on December 16 and a longer work stoppage on December 19.
If the groups decide to synchronise strikes, the action would likely bring the South Korean economic engine to a stop on whatever days were finally chosen over the next two weeks.

The strife comes at a time when South Korea is already burdened with low corporate earnings this year and plagued by plunging international prices for major exports, including memory chips, steel and petrochemical products.
The central Bank of Korea said the current account deficit would reach $22 billion this year, compared with a $8.95 shortfall in 1995.
It said gross domestic product growth would fall to 6.4 percent for all of 1997, from estimated growth of 6.9 percent this year and a 9.0 percent growth in 1995.
The stock market stood at 696.11 at the end of Saturday, the lowest since September 21, 1993, and most analysts expect the fall to continue to about 650 by the end of the year.

A Defence Ministry criminal complaint against South Korea's largest capitalised investment trust last Friday over a military pension fund was likely to lure more investors away from the depressed stock market.
Analysts said some investors would move to bonds, seen as a safer instrument in the present climate. Yields on three year benchmark corporate bonds rose to a new year high of 12.65 percent on Friday.

The complaint, which alleges fraud, claimed that when a nearly $50 million military pension fund was deposited with Daehan Investment Trust on January 16, 1995, Daehan employees issued a memorandum guaranteeing a minimum annual fixed rate of return of 15.7 to 20 percent through investment in bonds.
But instead of putting the money in bonds, Daehan invested it in shares resulting in a huge loss in return as the country's stock market lost value. Daehan has strongly denied any wrongdoing.
